name: Carriot
label: CARRIOT
title: Carriot.
lede: A cloud-based last-mile delivery and dispatch platform — I rebuilt its brand and redesigned the platform its dispatchers run the fleet from.

hero.alt: Carriot brand hero: the logo over a green landscape

meta.label: TEAM
meta.text: A three-person product team: a PM, a front-end developer, and me on design.

meta.label: SCOPE
meta.text: Brand book, logotype, illustration, fleet platform UI — 50+ screens, 30+ component UI kit

problem.label: THE PROBLEM
problem.title: Every new customer brought a requirement the last one never had — and all of them had to live in one panel.
paragraphs: Carriot was winning customers quickly, and the company’s strategy was to meet each fleet’s own logistics needs rather than sell one fixed workflow. A pharmaceutical distributor needed the cabin temperature recorded on the vehicle itself; a snack and beverage distributor needed to know the moment a driver left the delivery zone.

Each request arrived as one customer’s feature rather than a pattern, so the panel was growing by accretion. And the logistics team was attached to the manual routing it already trusted — so breadth and adoption were not two problems but one.

items.title: Rebuilt the identity from the mark out.
items.text: The old lettering fell apart at small sizes and could not survive an app icon or a single-colour print, so I rebuilt it on even weights and spacing. The illustration moved to 3D for the same reason: flat drawings were not carrying what the product actually moves.
items.cost: every 3D asset costs more production time than a flat one.

items.title: Made the panel configurable per customer, not per release.
items.text: Pharma fleets, snack routes and beverage distributors each needed something the others did not. Instead of one panel holding every control, the product became a core set of screens plus modules — cabin temperature, safe area, driver scoring — switched on per account.
items.cost: every module is one more thing sales has to scope and support has to explain.

items.title: Turned cargo theft into a design object: the safe area.
items.text: One customer kept losing cargo to drivers selling it en route. We made the safe area a first-class thing in the product — a zone set per vehicle, and a warning the moment it is left — so the alert arrives with a reason attached, not just a position.
items.cost: it puts drivers under watch, so the zone is scoped per vehicle rather than following the person all day.

items.title: Designed smart routing to advise the dispatcher, not replace them.
items.text: The hardest part was not the interface. The logistics team trusted its own routing, had interests tied to it, and read a smart system as a threat to the role. So the suggestion shows its reasoning and the dispatcher keeps the final assignment — and that is why they took it up.
items.cost: keeping a human in the loop caps how far the routing can optimise.

outcome.label: OUTCOME
outcome.title: The team that resisted smart routing ended up running on it.
outcome.text: Running costs came down and vehicles were allocated and spread better across the delivery area. The brand book and the website went live, and the platform work — 50+ screens and a 30+ component UI kit — became the reference the team built against, with modules that let one product serve fleets from pharmaceutical cold chain to snacks and beverages.
